name: Landing
description: Test how a lander descends, detects hazards and touches down. Earth tests focus on navigation, guidance and the behaviour of the surface under the vehicle.
briefing: A landing test campaign flies a vehicle (or a test bed) over a prepared zone, checks that sensors recognise slopes, rocks and craters, and verifies a safe touchdown. The terrain must look like the target from above and be safe enough to repeat the test many times.
siteNeeds: Clear skies for optical navigation tests
Few obstacles and little vegetation in the landing zone

vehicles.name: Kestrel-L light lander
vehicles.description: Small precision lander for navigation experiments.
vehicles.tradeoff: Very precise, but sensitive to dust and uneven ground.

vehicles.name: Atlas-H cargo lander
vehicles.description: Heavy lander concept for delivering base equipment.
vehicles.tradeoff: Needs a very flat, firm surface and is slow to retarget.

vehicles.name: Hopper-V vertical test bed
vehicles.tradeoff: Cheap repeated tests, but not a real descent from orbit.

options.label: Low sun angle
options.description: Long shadows, closer to lunar polar lighting.

options.label: Night
options.description: Tests lidar only; optical cameras blind.

options.label: Autonomous hazard avoidance
options.description: The vehicle picks its own landing spot.

options.label: Pilot-in-the-loop
options.description: A human confirms the final target.

name: Rover
description: Drive a robotic or crewed rover across terrain that looks and behaves like the Moon or Mars. Tests cover mobility, navigation, sampling and remote operations.
briefing: A rover campaign sends a vehicle across varied ground: loose regolith, rocks, slopes and obstacles. Operators often work from a distant control room with an artificial communication delay, and scientists choose where to drive and what to sample.
siteNeeds: Varied terrain: regolith, rocks, slopes, obstacles
Geology relevant to the target body

vehicles.name: Pathfinder-6 wheeled rover
vehicles.tradeoff: Reliable on gravel and rock, but can get stuck in loose sand.

vehicles.name: Strider wheel-leg rover
vehicles.description: Hybrid wheel-leg vehicle for steep, broken terrain.
vehicles.tradeoff: Climbs almost anything, but is complex and slow.

vehicles.name: Dune-Tracker tracked rover
vehicles.description: Tracked vehicle for soft and sandy ground.
vehicles.tradeoff: Great flotation in sand, but power-hungry and wears quickly on rock.

options.label: Dry season
options.description: Firm ground, dust, long field days.

options.label: Wet season
options.description: Mud and vegetation reduce the analog value.

options.label: Science traverse with sampling
options.description: Scientists pick targets along the way.

name: Base
description: Live and work in a habitat for days or months, as a crew would at a permanent Moon or Mars base. Tests cover isolation, life support, logistics and use of local resources.
briefing: A base analog places a small crew inside a habitat with limited supplies and communication. The crew runs experiments, makes excursions in simulated suits, and the team measures health, team dynamics and how well the systems hold up.
siteNeeds: Isolation from towns and daily life
Potential for in-situ resource use (ISRU) experiments

vehicles.name: Inflatable dome habitat
vehicles.tradeoff: Quick to deploy, but weaker thermal and radiation protection.

vehicles.name: Regolith-bermed module
vehicles.description: Rigid module covered with local soil.
vehicles.tradeoff: Best shielding, but needs local material and heavy equipment.

vehicles.name: Rigid container cluster
vehicles.tradeoff: Easy to ship anywhere, but leaks heat in extreme cold.

options.label: Harshest season
options.description: Maximum stress on crew and systems.

options.label: 6 months
options.description: Very realistic, high cost and risk.

options.label: Full isolation + comms delay
options.description: No outside contact except delayed messages.
